name: Victor Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Victor, and thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, how would you describe your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My brother Kwame and I farm Greenhill together, the farm our father built up after he bought it in the eighties. We milk 160 cows, grow wheat and barley, and keep a few beef calves off the dairy. He does the milking side, I do the crops, the youngstock and most of the selling. My wife Abena teaches at the primary school, and we've two children, Kofi who's twelve and Esi who's nine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm out by six with the young stock, then it's the field work: drilling, spraying, combining in August, depending on the season. I take one of the lads from the agricultural college two days a week as an apprentice, because that's how my father taught me and it's how it should be done. I like the rhythm of it, the year turning, the feeling at harvest supper. What wears me out is the milk price going up and down like a yo-yo, and the rules that change every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like every new thing, some of it's useful and most of it's talk. At the young farmers' club I'd tell them not to bet the farm on a gadget. Online I'd just share the odd article, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means we carry on as we are. The farm's in good shape, the savings are fine, the mortgage on our house in the village is coming down. That's good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. I'd keep using the GPS on the tractor and the AI bit on the milk recording software, which Kwame set up. Keep training the apprentice. Nothing new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the world I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any of the AI tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. The milk recording people put an AI thing in that spots cows going lame from the data, and Kwame uses it. I ask it questions sometimes, about spray timings. I waited till half the valley was using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want young farmers to take from this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That good farming is still about knowing your land and your animals. The tools help, but they don't replace a good stockman. And that the work is worth doing.

S0.say: I'd say it's like every new thing, some useful and most of it talk. At the young farmers' club I'd tell them not to bet the farm on a gadget.
S0.think: For me it means we carry on as we are, with the farm in good shape and the house mortgage coming down. That's good.
S0.do: Keeps using GPS steering and the AI tool in the milk recording software. Keeps training his college apprentice and changes nothing else.
S0.feel: Calm, in the world he knows.
S0.quote: The tools help, but they don't replace a good stockman.
S0.fieldNote: Victor talks like a mentor, focused on passing on good farming to young people. He uses AI tools sometimes, after most of the valley had them. He's content and stable in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's farming, it's always changed. You adapt or you get left behind. I'd say it at the club and at the market.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd be fine. We own the farm, we've got savings, and we'd buy what works once the neighbours had tried it. The ones I'd worry about are the hired men on the big estates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a couple of farms near us had them running for a year, we'd put in a robot milker, maybe two, around 150 thousand with a loan. I'd learn the software properly. And I'd keep the apprentice going, just training him on the new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit of excitement even, once it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Kwame buy first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot milker for Kwame, to give him his mornings back. He's not slept in since he was sixteen. I'd want to see one running on Dawson's farm first, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train him on the robots and the data. He'd be the one who knows both, the old way and the new. That's what an apprenticeship's for.

S1.say: I'd say that's farming, it's always changed, and you adapt or get left behind. I'd say it at the young farmers' club and at the market.
S1.think: I think we'd be fine because we own the farm, have savings and would buy what works once neighbours had tried it. I'd worry more about hired men on the big estates.
S1.do: Puts in one or two robot milkers, about 150 thousand with a loan, once nearby farms have run them for a year. Learns the software properly and trains the apprentice on the new kit.
S1.feel: Calm, even a bit excited once it's proven.
S1.quote: He's not slept in since he was sixteen.
S1.fieldNote: Victor would invest, but only after neighbours had proved the kit. He'd keep his apprentice and teach him both old and new ways. His worry is for hired workers on bigger estates, not his own family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and too reckless, and families and communities will pay for it. I'd say the churches and the farming groups need to look after their own. I'm not one for protests, but I'd speak up at the club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me. We own the land, so we wouldn't lose everything, but if robots do it all, what are Kwame and I for? And what does Abena do if robots can teach?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off big spending and keep the cash safe. I'd talk to Kwame about whether to buy robots fast or hold back, and I honestly don't know which. I'd look at the kids' schooling too, and maybe keep Kofi's college fund in the bank rather than shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, but I'd be praying on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very fast. What does that do to how you usually decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the trouble. I wait and see what works on Dawson's farm first. With two years, Dawson's in the same boat, nobody knows anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kofi and Esi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'll be all right as a family, because we will. The farm's ours, and we've got each other and the church. But I'd also tell them to be ready to work hard at whatever comes.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and reckless, and families and communities will pay for it. The churches and farming groups need to look after their own, and I'd speak up at the club.
S2.think: It worries me. We own the land, so we wouldn't lose everything, but if robots do it all, what are Kwame and I for, and what does Abena do if robots can teach?
S2.do: Holds off big spending and keeps cash safe. Talks with his brother about whether to buy robots fast or wait, and moves his son's college fund from shares into the bank.
S2.feel: Anxious but not panicked, praying on it.
S2.quote: With two years, Dawson's in the same boat, nobody knows anything.
S2.fieldNote: Victor's usual method, waiting for a neighbour to prove things, fails here. Owning the land protects his family's base, but his sense of purpose and his wife's teaching job are exposed. He leans on church and family in his words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to prepare, so let's do it properly. Farmers should help each other through it, like we always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough for us. We'd automate once it's proven, keep the land, and make sure the family's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one or two, we'd watch what the early farms do. By year three, we'd buy the robots that work, with savings and a loan. I'd keep the apprentice on and push the college to train young farmers for the new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I won't lie. But it's the kind of worry you can plan around, like a wet forecast at harvest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years instead of two. What changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can see it working on Dawson's place before I buy. That's how I like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who outside your family would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young lads at the club. They're starting out, no land, no savings. I'd want the college and the farming groups to give them a path.

S3.say: I'd say we've got time to prepare, so let's do it properly. Farmers should help each other through it, like we always have.
S3.think: I think five years is enough for us: we'd automate once it's proven, keep the land and make sure the family's fine.
S3.do: Watches early adopters for the first two years, then buys proven robots by year three with savings and a loan. Keeps the apprentice and pushes the local college to train young farmers on the new kit.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but the kind of worry he can plan around.
S3.quote: Five years means I can see it working on Dawson's place before I buy.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Victor his preferred pace: watch, then buy. His concern moves to young farmers without land or savings. He'd push training through the college, in line with his belief in apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do it right. Train the young ones, look after families, keep the land in good hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine. I'd be 53, mortgage nearly gone, kids grown. We'd automate the farm and keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now, I'd start setting money aside for robots and keep learning the tools bit by bit. By year five, I'd buy the kit that's proven. I'd keep the apprentice scheme going and help the kids plan for the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly settled. Abena says I worry like my father, quietly and with a notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. What would you start now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The work itself. My father's hands were like leather. Mine will be soft by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: And the harvest supper. If there's no harvest crew, who do you feed?

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to do it right. Train the young ones, look after families and keep the land in good hands.
S4.think: I'd be fine at 53 with the mortgage nearly gone and the kids grown. We'd automate the farm and keep going.
S4.do: Sets money aside for robots now and learns the tools bit by bit. Buys proven kit by year five, keeps the apprentice scheme going and helps the children plan ahead.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly settled, with sadness about losing the physical work.
S4.quote: My father's hands were like leather. Mine will be soft by then.
S4.fieldNote: Victor is practical and secure about money with ten years, but feels the loss of physical work and farm traditions. His mention of the harvest supper shows how much community matters to him.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I can't wait and see how it goes for others. What would help is the government giving farmers time and fair rules, and the colleges training young people on the new kit so they're not left out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the young ones. Everyone talks about jobs, but who teaches the next lot how to farm? That's what I care about.

headlineQuote: If there's no harvest crew, who do you feed?
portrait: Victor Mensah is a 43-year-old farmer who runs Greenhill, a dairy and cereal farm, with his brother Kwame. He's married to Abena, a primary teacher, and has two children. He uses AI tools sometimes, after neighbours have proved them, and trains a college apprentice. He's calm in the first two pictures and would invest in robot milkers once proven. Fast AGI makes him anxious because there's no one to watch first, while five and ten years let him automate at his own pace. He cares about young farmers and community traditions.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he couldn't wait and see how it worked for others first.
whatWouldHelp: Time and fair rules from government, and colleges training young people on the new kit.
